syllabus.clause: Tarjan's low-link single pass vs Kosaraju's two passes

at.step: Tarjan's algorithm runs a single depth-first search, maintaining a low-link value per vertex — the smallest discovery index reachable from it through tree and back edges — and pops a complete component the instant a vertex's low-link equals its own discovery index.

Kosaraju's algorithm runs DFS once to get a finish order, reverses every edge, and runs DFS again in decreasing finish order. Each new DFS tree in the second pass is exactly one strongly connected component — simpler to state, at the cost of a second full pass and an explicit transpose.
Contracting every strongly connected component of any directed graph down to a single vertex — is the result always a DAG, sometimes a DAG, or never a DAG?

Contracting every strongly connected component to a single vertex turns any directed graph into a DAG. A cycle among the condensed vertices would mean their original components were mutually reachable — contradicting that each was already a maximal such group.

In a two-SAT instance's implication graph, if a variable's two literals (itself and its negation) land in the same strongly connected component, is the formula satisfiable, unsatisfiable, or does it depend on the rest of the formula?

items.item: Tarjan's and Kosaraju's algorithms must agree on the exact partition into SCCs, not merely on the count of components, since the SCC partition of a graph is unique regardless of which algorithm finds it

items.item: The condensation-is-a-DAG proof is a maximality argument, not a graph-search argument: it holds because SCCs are defined as maximal mutually-reachable sets, so two components reaching each other both ways would contradict their own definition

items.item: Both SCC algorithms run in O(n + m): Tarjan's is one DFS pass with constant extra work per vertex and edge; Kosaraju's is exactly two such passes plus a linear-time transpose construction

at.step: A graph where every vertex can reach every other looks, from a distance, indistinguishable from one where only small pockets can reach each other. Telling the two apart, for a graph with a billion edges, takes exactly one more depth-first search, carrying one extra number per vertex.

items.item: This topic closes the chapter's own arc: BFS and DFS as the two traversal orders, and every later structural fact (shortest paths, topological order, SCCs) as a side effect of one of those two traversals rather than a new kind of search

at.step: Finding one key, one boundary, one order statistic was the previous chapter's business. This chapter answered a different kind of question about a graph with no weights at all: which vertices are reachable, in what order, and which groups of vertices can all reach each other. Every answer cost exactly one traversal.
